Mathematical Formulation¶

This page describes the continuous equations solved by LilyTorch. For discrete stencils and time-stepping details see Numerical Schemes.

Governing equations¶

LilyTorch solves the incompressible Navier–Stokes equations in the velocity–pressure formulation:

(1)¶\[\frac{\partial \mathbf{u}}{\partial t} + (\mathbf{u}\cdot\nabla)\mathbf{u} = -\frac{1}{\rho}\,\nabla p + \nu\,\nabla^{2}\mathbf{u}\]
(2)¶\[\nabla\cdot\mathbf{u} = 0\]

where

  • \(\mathbf{u}=(u,v)\) (2-D) or \((u,v,w)\) (3-D) is the velocity field,

  • \(p\) is the pressure,

  • \(\rho\) is the (constant) fluid density,

  • \(\nu\) is the kinematic viscosity.

Fractional-step pressure projection¶

The divergence-free constraint (2) is enforced by a pressure-projection (Chorin–Témam) step. After computing a provisional velocity \(\tilde{\mathbf{u}}\) that satisfies the momentum equation without the pressure gradient, a Poisson equation is solved for the pressure correction:

(3)¶\[\nabla\cdot\!\left(\frac{w\,\Delta t}{\rho}\,\mu_0\,\nabla p\right) = \nabla\cdot\tilde{\mathbf{u}}\]

and the velocity is corrected:

(4)¶\[\mathbf{u}^{n+1} = \tilde{\mathbf{u}} - \frac{w\,\Delta t}{\rho}\,\mu_0\,\nabla p\]

The weight \(w\) depends on the Runge–Kutta stage (\(w=1\) in the predictor, \(w=\tfrac12\) in the corrector; see Time integration — Heun’s method (RK2)).

The mask function \(\mu_0\) equals 1 in the fluid and smoothly transitions to 0 inside immersed bodies (see Immersed Boundary Method — BDIM2). In the absence of bodies, \(\mu_0\equiv 1\) and equation (3) reduces to the standard constant-coefficient Poisson equation.

Poisson equation — FFT approach (Neumann)¶

When all domain boundaries carry Neumann conditions (\(\partial p/\partial n = 0\)), a spectral solve is used via the Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT-II, Makhoul 1980).

The eigenvalues of the discrete Laplacian under Neumann BCs are

\[\lambda_k = \frac{2}{h^{2}} \!\left(\cos\!\left(\frac{\pi k}{N}\right) - 1\right), \qquad k = 0, 1, \dots, N-1\]

The solution is: DCT-II \(\to\) divide by eigenvalues \(\to\) inverse DCT-II, yielding spectral accuracy for a smooth right-hand side.

Poisson equation — FFT approach (free-space)¶

For unbounded (free-space) domains the solver computes the discrete convolution of the right-hand side with a regularised Green’s function via zero-padded FFTs.

2-D Green’s function (Hejlesen et al. 2013, 8th-order algebraic smoothing):

\[\begin{split}G(r) = \frac{1}{2\pi} \begin{cases} \displaystyle -\tfrac{1}{2}\ln(r^{2}+\sigma^{2}) + \sum_{k=1}^{4} \frac{1}{2k} \frac{\sigma^{2k}}{(r^{2}+\sigma^{2})^{k}} & r > 0 \\[6pt] \displaystyle -\tfrac{1}{2}\ln(\sigma^{2}) + \sum_{k=1}^{4} \frac{1}{2k} & r = 0 \end{cases}\end{split}\]

3-D Green’s function (Gaussian/erf regularisation):

\[G(r) = -\frac{1}{4\pi r}\, \operatorname{erf}\!\left(\frac{r}{\sqrt{2}\,\sigma}\right)\]

where \(\sigma = h\) is the grid spacing.

Poisson equation — variable-coefficient (multigrid)¶

When immersed bodies are present (\(\mu_0 \neq 1\)), the Poisson equation (3) becomes variable-coefficient:

\[\nabla\cdot(c\,\nabla p) = f\]

Discrete stencil along dimension \(d\):

\[\frac{c_{d+}\,p_{i+1} - (c_{d+}+c_{d-})\,p_{i} + c_{d-}\,p_{i-1}}{h^{2}}\]

where face coefficients \(c_{d\pm}\) are the harmonic averages of \(\mu_0\) evaluated at cell faces. This is solved by geometric multigrid V-cycles or a multigrid-preconditioned conjugate-gradient (MGCG) iteration (see Poisson solvers).

Variable-density pressure projection¶

In coupled FARMS simulations the body may have a different density \(\rho_b\) from the fluid \(\rho_f\). The effective density is

\[\rho(\mathbf{x}) = \rho_b + (\rho_f - \rho_b)\,\mu_0(\mathbf{x})\]

In this coupled variable-density extension the face-centred coefficients are

\[c_u = \frac{\Delta t}{\rho_u}, \qquad c_v = \frac{\Delta t}{\rho_v}, \qquad c_w = \frac{\Delta t}{\rho_w}\]

with \(\rho_u, \rho_v, \rho_w\) the BDIM-blended densities on the staggered face grids. The corresponding cell-centred FFT coefficient is \(c_{cc} = \Delta t / \rho_{cc}\).

This coupled FARMS formulation differs from upstream WaterLily’s built-in single-density operator. When \(\rho_b = \rho_f\), the default BDIM / WaterLily form reduces to \((w\Delta t / \rho_f)\,\mu_0\); when the body density is blended explicitly into \(\rho\), lilytorch uses the effective-density coefficients above for the custom multigrid path.

These two coefficient fields are not algebraically identical rewrites of one another. With

\[\rho(\mu_0) = \rho_b + (\rho_f - \rho_b)\,\mu_0\]

we have, in general,

\[\frac{\mu_0}{\rho(\mu_0)} \neq \frac{1}{\rho(\mu_0)}\]

except in the trivial fluid region \(\mu_0 = 1\). Therefore LilyTorch’s custom FARMS variable-density operator should be understood as a separate extension that shares WaterLily’s BDIM fields and single-density limit, not as the exact same variable-coefficient operator under a different pressure scaling.

Advection–diffusion¶

The advection–diffusion sub-step advances each velocity component by one Forward-Euler step:

\[u^{*} = u^{n} + \Delta t \left[ -\nabla\cdot(\mathbf{u}\otimes u) + \nu\,\nabla^{2} u \right]\]

The CFL stability condition is

\[\Delta t \le \frac{\min(h)}{v_{\max} + 3\nu}\]

Smagorinsky LES model (optional)¶

When the grid is too coarse to resolve all turbulent scales, an optional Smagorinsky subgrid-scale (SGS) model (Smagorinsky 1963) can be enabled. It models the effect of unresolved eddies as an additive eddy viscosity \(\nu_t\):

(5)¶\[\nu_t = (C_s \, \Delta)^{2} \, |\bar{S}|\]

where

  • \(C_s\) is the Smagorinsky constant (typically 0.1–0.2),

  • \(\Delta\) is the grid filter width (taken equal to the grid spacing \(h\)),

  • \(|\bar{S}| = \sqrt{2\,\bar{S}_{ij}\,\bar{S}_{ij}}\) is the magnitude of the resolved strain-rate tensor

    \[\bar{S}_{ij} = \frac{1}{2} \left( \frac{\partial \bar{u}_i}{\partial x_j} + \frac{\partial \bar{u}_j}{\partial x_i} \right)\]

With this model the diffusion term in the momentum equation becomes

(6)¶\[\nabla \cdot \bigl[(\nu + \nu_t) \, \nabla \mathbf{u}\bigr]\]

instead of \(\nu\,\nabla^{2}\mathbf{u}\). Because \(\nu_t\) varies in space (it depends on the local velocity gradients), this requires a variable-coefficient Laplacian; see Numerical Schemes for the discrete stencil.

The CFL condition is likewise updated:

\[\Delta t \le \frac{\min(h)}{v_{\max} + 3(\nu + \max\,\nu_t)}\]

The model is disabled by default (\(C_s = 0\)). When disabled, the solver reverts exactly to the standard constant-viscosity formulation with zero computational overhead. To enable, set smagorinsky_cs in the YAML configuration; see Configuration Reference.

Non-Newtonian viscosity (optional)¶

In addition to constant kinematic viscosity, LilyTorch supports two spatially-varying viscosity models. When active, the constant nu is overridden by a field recomputed every time-step from the local strain rate \(\dot\gamma = |\bar S|\) (see (5)).

Note

Non-Newtonian viscosity and Smagorinsky LES cannot be used simultaneously — both provide a variable effective viscosity and would otherwise compound.

Carreau model (shear-thinning)¶

For shear-thinning fluids (CMC, polymer solutions) whose viscosity decreases with shear rate:

(7)¶\[\nu(\dot\gamma) = \nu_\infty + (\nu_0 - \nu_\infty)\, \bigl[\,1 + (\lambda\,\dot\gamma)^{2}\,\bigr]^{(n-1)/2}\]

with

  • \(\nu_0\) — zero-shear kinematic viscosity [m²/s],

  • \(\nu_\infty\) — infinite-shear kinematic viscosity [m²/s],

  • \(\lambda\) — relaxation time [s]; thinning begins around \(\dot\gamma_c \approx 1/\lambda\),

  • \(n\) — power-law index; \(n = 1\) recovers the Newtonian limit, \(n \to 0\) gives strong thinning.

Herschel–Bulkley extension (yield stress)¶

A yield stress \(\tau_y\) added on top of (7) prevents flow below a critical stress — useful for gels and concentrated polymer solutions that behave as soft solids at rest:

\[\nu_\text{eff}(\dot\gamma) = \nu_\text{Carreau}(\dot\gamma) + \frac{\tau_y}{\rho\,\max(\dot\gamma,\,\epsilon)}\]

A CFL-based upper clamp nu_max is computed automatically so that the diverging \(1/\dot\gamma\) term never violates the diffusion stability limit.

Sponge / damping layer (optional)¶

A sponge layer absorbs outgoing waves and suppresses spurious recirculation near domain boundaries — effectively mimicking an infinite domain. This is important for low-Reynolds / Stokes-like flows where the pressure Poisson equation instantaneously propagates velocity across the entire domain.

A damping coefficient \(\sigma(\mathbf{x})\) is defined on the grid, ramping from zero in the interior up to \(\sigma_\text{max}\) near each wall using a smooth quadratic profile:

\[\sigma(\mathbf{x}) = \sigma_\text{max}\, \left(\frac{\max(0,\; L_s - d)}{L_s}\right)^{2}\]

where \(d\) is the distance to the nearest domain boundary and \(L_s\) is the sponge thickness. After each pressure projection the velocity is damped in place:

\[\mathbf{u} \leftarrow \frac{\mathbf{u}}{1 + \Delta t\,\sigma(\mathbf{x})}\]

In the interior (\(d > L_s\)) \(\sigma = 0\) and physics is unchanged. Near walls \(\sigma\) ramps up and drives the velocity toward zero. The layer thickness and strength are exposed through the YAML config; see Configuration Reference.

Force computation¶

Hydrodynamic forces on immersed bodies are computed by integrating the stress tensor over the body surface using smoothed delta functions.

Viscous forces (contour integral):

\[\mathbf{F}_{\text{visc}} = \int (\boldsymbol{\sigma}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{n}})\; \delta_{\varepsilon}(d - \varepsilon)\,\mathrm{d}V\]

Pressure forces:

\[\mathbf{F}_{\text{pres}} = -\int p\,\hat{\mathbf{n}}\; \delta_{\varepsilon}(d)\,\mathrm{d}V\]

where the smoothed delta function is

\[\delta_{\varepsilon}(d) = \frac{1+\cos(\pi d/\varepsilon)}{2\varepsilon}\]

Torque decomposition (avoids constructing the full moment-arm tensor):

\[\tau_x = \sum(Y\,f_z)\,h^{3} - \mathrm{com}_y\,F_z - \sum(Z\,f_y)\,h^{3} + \mathrm{com}_z\,F_y\]

Buoyancy (FARMS coupling)¶

In the coupled MuJoCo mode, buoyancy on each link is computed as

\[F_{z,\text{buoy}} = -\rho_{\text{water}}\, \frac{m_{\text{link}}}{\rho_{\text{body}}}\,g \cdot \min\!\left( \frac{z_{\text{surface}} + h_{\text{link}} - z_{\text{link}}} {2\,h_{\text{link}}},\;1 \right)\]
